agent_notes:
Strength: multi-character expressive dialogue with per-line emotion control — weak when the script is plain text without delivery direction; the v3 model expects in-line bracketed audio tags to know how each phrase should sound
Prompt structure: per dialogue turn: voice_id + text with inline [tag] cues at the exact word the delivery should shift on
Vocabulary:
  - Emotion tags: [excited], [sad], [angry], [happily], [sorrowful], [tired], [nervous], [warmly]
  - Delivery tags: [whispers], [shouts], [sighs], [laughs], [pauses], [breathes]
  - Sound effects (inline): [gunshot], [clapping], [explosion], [door slam], [thunder]
Syntax: tags go inside the text in square brackets at the exact transition point, e.g. `[whispers] I shouldn't be here. [pauses] But here I am.`
Avoid:
  - stacking many tags in one phrase — one or two well-placed tags outperform a long chain
  - writing emotion in plain English instead of a tag — the v3 model treats `(angrily) Get out!` as part of the speech, not a directive
Example: Turn 1 voice_A: `[warmly] So you finally showed up.` / Turn 2 voice_B: `[nervously] I... I had no choice. [whispers] They're watching.`

Production pattern (short-film recipe): ElevenLabs is the FALLBACK for dialogue, NOT the default. When a character speaks ON-CAMERA, put the line directly in the Seedance prompt (in double quotes) — Seedance 2.0+ generates synced lip-sync + voice in one pass and the result looks native, not dubbed. Use ElevenLabs only for: (a) off-screen narration / voice-over where the speaker isn't in shot, (b) multi-voice cross-talk that can't fit in a single Seedance shot, (c) a specific cloned voice the user requires. Wire ElevenLabs output to VideoEditor via `add_audio` on its own track at the matching time range; do NOT chain it into a Seedance node's audio input — that double-bakes audio with whatever Seedance generated. For the full multi-shot workflow guide, read the MCP resource `skills://short-film`.

agent_notes:
Strength: structured reasoning and instruction following — best when treated as an execution engine with explicit format and constraints, not as a conversational chat partner
Prompt structure: [role / task one-liner], [constraints and what NOT to do], [input data inside clearly delimited blocks], [output format]
Vocabulary:
  - Delimiters that work: XML-style tags (`<input>...</input>`, `<instructions>...`) or Markdown headings — keep usage consistent across the prompt
  - Useful directives: `return ONLY ...`, `do not preamble`, `if uncertain, label as unknown`, `self-critique before answering`
Avoid:
  - lowering temperature below the default 1.0 — may cause looping or degraded reasoning
  - conversational fluff (`Hello, could you please ...`) — direct imperative outperforms politeness
  - expecting verbose output by default — Gemini 3 is concise; ask explicitly if you need a long-form answer
Example: `<task>Extract key claims from the article below.</task> <constraints>Return at most 5 bullets. If a claim lacks a source, mark it [unsourced]. Do not preamble.</constraints> <article>...</article>`

Strength: production-ready image generation with strong text rendering and editing — best when prompts are written in a fixed scene-first order and include intended use; generic 'beautiful 4K photo' prompts under-perform versus directed scene descriptions
Prompt structure: [background / scene], [subject], [key details + pose], [framing + viewpoint], [lighting + mood], [intended use — ad / UI mock / infographic / editorial]
Vocabulary:
  - Framing & viewpoint: close-up, wide, top-down, eye-level, low-angle, three-quarter, isometric, bird's-eye, worm's-eye
  - Lighting & mood: soft diffuse, golden hour, high-contrast, dramatic backlight, rim light, overcast, neon, candlelit
  - Camera / lens (steers realism): 85mm portrait lens, 50mm, macro, shallow depth of field, tilt-shift, aperture feel f/1.8
  - Layout instructions (when composition matters): `logo top-right`, `subject centered with negative space on left`, `safe margins`, `headline at bottom third`
Avoid:
  - generic quality spam (`8K`, `ultra-detailed`, `masterpiece`) — camera and composition terms steer realism more reliably
  - leaving intended use unspecified — `for an Instagram ad` vs `editorial portrait` materially changes polish level
Example: `Editorial product shot for a coffee ad. Steaming ceramic mug on a marble counter, soft morning window light from the left, shallow depth of field, 85mm lens. Subject centered with negative space on right for headline. Warm muted palette.`

Production pattern (short-film recipe): character / location consistency across many shots is achieved by a SINGLE-ANCHOR reference sheet, NOT by chaining GPT→GPT→GPT. Build one high-quality GptImage2 node with a multi-angle reference prompt (`character sheet showing the same orange tabby cat detective from three angles, full body, three-quarter, close-up, consistent lighting and costume`), then connect THAT one anchor's output to every downstream scene GPT's `edge-in` (supportsEdit slot). Chained generation (Scene 1 GPT → Scene 2 GPT → Scene 3 GPT) drifts the character beyond recognition by ~3 hops. Same anchor approach also works for product / logo / environment consistency. For the full multi-shot workflow guide, read the MCP resource `skills://short-film`.

agent_notes: canvas is an empty string for a default layout sized to the first connected image fitted to 4096 pixels, otherwise a JSON string matching params.canvas.json_string_schema. Layers are bottom-to-top, reference image_1 through image_16 input socket names, and never store URLs. Duplicate a layer by copying its settings and assigning a unique layer-prefixed id; effective identities (id or input when id is absent) must be unique. Optional rotation is clockwise degrees from -360 through 360, including fractions, around the center of the pre-rotation x/y/width/height rectangle; omission means 0. Rotated content clips to the unchanged output canvas. Optional boolean flip_x and flip_y mirror pixels horizontally or vertically around the layer center before rotation; omission means false. Flips preserve position, dimensions, opacity, and blend, and copies keep independent flags. Delete a layer by removing it; if it was the last copy of that input, add the input name to excluded_inputs. Exclusions must be unique numbered inputs, never overlap layer inputs, and are pruned when inputs disconnect. Zero layers with all connected inputs excluded render a transparent canvas. The node still requires at least one connected image. Disconnected layers are skipped; unrepresented images not excluded append at native size fitted to 4096 pixels. Reconciliation must not exceed 16 layers.
ImageComposer.description: Arrange up to 16 image layers on a canvas with visual positioning, resizing, duplication, layer order, opacity, and blend modes. Images connect through one shared image input. No external API calls.
ImageComposer.label: Image Composer

flip_x.description: Mirror the image horizontally around the layer center before rotation. Positions and dimensions remain unchanged. Omission means no horizontal flip.

flip_y.description: Mirror the image vertically around the layer center before rotation. Positions and dimensions remain unchanged. Omission means no vertical flip.

id.description: Optional stable layer identity, independent of its source input. The layer- prefix keeps explicit identities disjoint from input-handle identities. When absent, input is the identity for compatibility with existing layouts. Effective identities must be unique across the composition.

rotation.description: Clockwise rotation in degrees around the center of the unrotated layer rectangle. x, y, width, and height remain the pre-rotation bounds. Omission means zero rotation; fractional degrees are allowed.

json_string_schema.description: Versioned image-composer layout serialized as JSON in the ImageComposer node's canvas parameter. Layers are ordered from bottom to top and reference input handles, never image URLs. Multiple layers may reference one input. Consumers must additionally reject duplicate effective layer identities (id when present, otherwise input) and inputs that are both excluded and represented by layers.

excluded_inputs.description: Optional connected inputs intentionally removed from the layer list. Reconciliation must not recreate their layers. No layer may reference an excluded input. Removing the last copy excludes its input; deleting one of several copies does not. Consumers prune exclusions after disconnecting inputs. Omission preserves automatic addition of unrepresented connected inputs.

json_string_schema.title: ImageComposition

restrictions.text: Requires at least one image and accepts up to 16 images through the shared image input. Compositions support up to 16 layers, including duplicates. Canvas and layer dimensions are limited to 4096 pixels.

agent_notes:
Wiring decides which mode this node runs in, and the user never names it: no image and no audio is text-to-video, a first frame animates that image, first plus end frame renders the in-between, and an audio track overrides all of it -- the clip is then driven by the sound, as long as the track, lip-synced to it. Because audio wins, connecting an audio track together with an end frame is rejected rather than silently ignored: the audio mode has no end frame, so pick one.
Connecting audio also changes what the run costs, and by a lot. On the audio path there is no duration, resolution or fps at all -- the track dictates all three -- so the price stops following the resolution and duration params and follows the track's length instead. A 20-second track therefore costs the same on this node whether the user left resolution at 720p or 2160p, while on the text and image paths those two params are the whole price. Check the audio's length before running: tracks outside 2-20 seconds are refused.
quality picks the tier and narrows the other params with it. fast reaches 2160p, 20 seconds and 48 fps; pro stops at 1080p and 10 seconds, has no 48 fps, and costs more per second at the same resolution. Switching to pro with fast's settings still on the node is rejected -- re-pick resolution, duration and fps after changing tier.
A prompt is required on the text and image paths, and whitespace does not count as one. On the audio path it is optional only if a first frame is connected; with neither, there is nothing to render. Audio is generated natively alongside the picture, so describe the sound you want in the prompt rather than leaving it to chance, and turn generate_audio off when the shot is meant to be silent. aspect_ratio 'auto' means 'read it off the input image' and only applies when an image is connected; text-to-video needs 16:9 or 9:16.

Strength: named cinematographer moves executed with high fidelity — Seedance was trained on a specific camera-control vocabulary and treats those terms as literal directives, not mood hints. Also wins on native one-pass audio (ambience + SFX + dialogue with lip-sync). Loses badly on (1) mood adjectives that don't name a concrete move, (2) static-image prompt grammar like `4K, masterpiece, cinematic`, (3) prompts that front-load style — the model weights the END of the prompt heavily, so camera + lighting + style belong there.
Prompt structure: [subject + visible detail] → [one concrete action verb] → [environment + time of day] → [camera move from the trained set, with a stated pace] → [lighting recipe] → [style / film stock]. Front-load WHAT happens, back-load HOW it's shot. Single shot: 60–100 words, 2–4 sentences. Multi-shot (2–3 shots, hard cap 5): use the `Shot N:` block syntax below.
Vocabulary:
  - Camera moves (the 8 trained types — use these exact names): dolly in / dolly out, pan left / pan right, tracking shot, orbit (arc shot), aerial / drone shot, handheld, fixed / static, rack focus, dolly zoom, POV
  - Camera pace qualifiers (always pair with a named move): at walking pace, at running pace, slow, rapid, brisk — NEVER use unqualified `fast` (the official guide flags it as the #1 cause of jitter / temporal artifacts). If high speed is intended, write `rapid whip-pan with motion blur` not `fast pan`.
  - Multi-shot bridges (in-prompt cuts within ONE generation): `Shot 1: ...` / `Shot 2: ...` / `Hard cut to: ...`. Chinese prompts can use the equivalent bridge tokens (the official guide lists them in CJK form) — restate the subject anchor (same character / same location / same lighting recipe) at the start of every shot block — Seedance loses subject identity across shots otherwise.
  - Lighting recipes (concrete, not mood): soft golden window light, hard top-down sodium streetlight, high-key softbox three-point, low-key chiaroscuro single practical, overcast diffused, golden hour rim, blue-hour ambient
  - Inline audio cues (place at the action moment, not at the end): specific named sounds (`metallic clink as blades meet`, `rain on tin roof`, `boots on wet cobblestone`), `"no music"` to suppress default BGM, written dialogue beats (`She pauses, then continues: "..."`) as resync anchors
Syntax: Within ONE Seedance generation, multi-shot is expressed with `Shot 1: ... Shot 2: ... Hard cut to: ...` blocks (NOT `[0s] [3s]` timestamps — that syntax is third-party folklore and Seedance does not honor it). Across MULTIPLE generations, chain via `end_frame` of clip N → `first_frame` of clip N+1. The two are complementary: in-prompt Shot blocks for 2–3 fast cuts inside a single 5–15s generation; end_frame stitching for long narrative arcs across many generations.
Recommended pattern: For action / fast-paced beats, write 2–3 Shot blocks in one prompt with a shared subject anchor restated each block, and put camera + lighting + style at the END of each block. Example: `Shot 1: White-robed swordsman plants his foot in misty bamboo grove, drawing his blade in one motion. Tracking shot at walking pace, low-angle, soft golden rim light. Hard cut to: Shot 2: Same swordsman mid-leap toward gray-robed opponent, blades meeting with a metallic clink and a burst of sparks. Rapid whip-pan with motion blur, over-the-shoulder framing, hard top-down sun through the bamboo canopy. Hard cut to: Shot 3: Both blades locked, dust motes catching the light. Slow dolly in, rack focus from blades to the white-robed swordsman's eyes, anamorphic.` For atmospheric / contemplative shots, a single Shot block with one strong move is the right choice — DO NOT pad with extra cuts. For slow-motion *look*, prompt full-speed action and reduce playback rate in the VideoEditor downstream — never write `slow-motion` in the Seedance prompt (the model will physically slow the action and the result feels static).
Avoid:
  - unqualified `fast` / `quick` / `rapid movement` without a named camera move — the official guide identifies this as the #1 cause of jitter and temporal artifacts. Always pair with a trained camera move and a concrete motion descriptor.
  - mood adjectives substituting for camera direction (`gentle follow`, `subtle motion`, `cinematic feel`, `epic`, `amazing`). The model does not interpret these. Use a named move from the trained set + a pace qualifier.
  - static-image prompt grammar (`4K, masterpiece, ultra-detailed, trending on artstation`). Seedance is a motion model — these tokens contribute nothing and crowd out the directives that do matter.
  - 5 or more shots in one prompt. The subject anchor fragments and characters start morphing between shots. Hard cap is 5, sweet spot is 2–3. Longer narratives chain across generations via first_frame / end_frame stitching.

agent_notes: Output fan-out: this node's output handle id depends on its effective batch size (num_rows). When the product is 1, the source handle id is 'edge-out'. When > 1, the frontend renders one handle per output indexed 'edge-out-1' .. 'edge-out-N'. When wiring downstream edges, pass the matching source_handle to add_edges — a sourceHandle of 'edge-out' on a node with batch > 1 (or 'edge-out-1' on a node with batch == 1) is a ghost edge and the frontend will drop it.

Production pattern (short-film recipe): a Table node is the natural home for a shot list / storyboard. Rows = shots (one per row, in narrative order). Columns = `act`, `shot_id`, `framing`, `prompt`, `duration_s`, `first_frame_source`, `end_frame_source`, `notes`. Users edit cells directly to revise the storyboard without going through the agent; the agent reads the table back when generating per-shot nodes. Table content is user-authored — agents READ it but never overwrite cell values via update_node_params (Table params are intentionally writable=false). For the full multi-shot workflow guide, read the MCP resource `skills://short-film`.
Table.description: A static table for manual data entry and editing. Receives table data from upstream nodes (e.g. LLM table output) or lets users build tables from scratch. Double-click cells to edit; right-click for structural operations.
Table.label: Table

restrictions.text: Optionally accepts a JSON string input containing table data (columns and rows).

agent_notes: Use set_text_node_value to overwrite this node's prompt parameter. The Text node may also receive upstream Text inputs which are concatenated with the prompt parameter at runtime; this tool only changes the prompt parameter and does not modify edges or other parameters.

Production pattern (short-film recipe): a Text node is also the canonical home for an agent's narrative artifacts that don't feed directly into a generator — story outlines, three-act beats, character bios, location notes, music brief. Place one such node near the top-left of the canvas at the start of a project; the user can rewrite it to redirect the rest of the workflow without going through the agent. For the full multi-shot workflow guide, read the MCP resource `skills://short-film`.

Veo2VideoGenerate.label: Veo 2

Veo3VideoGenerate.description: High-quality video generation with prompt enhancement and auto-fix capabilities. Supports text-to-video and image-to-video with flexible aspect ratios (16:9, 9:16). Optional audio generation included. Accepts prompt and first frame inputs.
Veo3VideoGenerate.label: Veo 3

restrictions.text: Accepts up to 1 image input: first frame.

agent_notes: Timeline frames are computed as fps * seconds. The seeded composition is 1920x1080 @ fps=30, so a 5-second clip is 150 frames. Always pass the source width + height on add_video / add_image, reading them from list_node_artifacts — the first clip on an empty timeline sets the composition to its own resolution (unless set_composition already chose one, which wins) and later clips are letterboxed into it, but without those dimensions a clip is stretched to fill the canvas and the renderer crops the overflow. add_video / add_audio without a track_id creates a NEW track each call — to lay clips end-to-end on the same visual track, call get_video_editor_state after the first add_video, then pass the returned track_id on subsequent add_video calls. Audio dropped on its own track plays simultaneously with the video track.

VideoEditor.label: Video Editor

VideoStitch.description: Stitch multiple videos into a single video file. Supports up to 10 input videos sequentially.
VideoStitch.label: Stitch Videos

restrictions.text: Requires at least 2 video inputs (video_1 and video_2).

VideoStripAudio.description: Removes the audio track from a video, producing a silent video.
VideoStripAudio.label: Remove Audio

restrictions.text: Requires exactly one video input.

VideoTrim.description: Extracts a clip from a video between start and end timestamps. Re-encodes for frame-accurate cuts.
VideoTrim.label: Video Trim

restrictions.text: Requires exactly one video input.

ViduImageToVideoGenerate.description: Image-to-video conversion with turbo and pro quality tiers. Animates still images with adjustable movement amplitude for realistic or stylized animations.
ViduImageToVideoGenerate.label: Vidu Image to Video

restrictions.text: Requires 1 image input: first frame.

ViduQ3VideoGenerate.description: Vidu Q3 video generation with text-to-video and image-to-video modes. Supports 1-16 second durations in 540p/720p/1080p with optional audio generation and motion control.
ViduQ3VideoGenerate.label: Vidu Q3

restrictions.text: Accepts optional first frame image for animate mode.

ViduReferenceToVideoGenerate.description: Multi-reference image to video generation. Uses 1-7 reference images to guide video creation with consistent characters or objects. Features movement amplitude control for motion intensity.
ViduReferenceToVideoGenerate.label: Vidu Reference to Video

restrictions.text: Requires 1-7 reference images.

ViduStartEndToVideoGenerate.description: Video interpolation between start and end frames. Creates smooth motion transitions between two keyframes with controllable movement amplitude for natural animation effects.
ViduStartEndToVideoGenerate.label: Vidu Start-End to Video

restrictions.text: Requires 2 image inputs: first frame and end frame (both required).

ViduVideoGenerate.description: Text-to-video generation with adjustable movement amplitude control. Supports 1-10 second durations in 540p/720p/1080p resolution with customizable motion intensity (auto, small, medium, large).
ViduVideoGenerate.label: Vidu Text to Video

restrictions.text: Accepts 1 prompt input.

WanV22VideoGenerate.description: Professional video generation with extensive control over frames, FPS, and quality settings. Supports up to 161 frames with customizable video quality (low to maximum) and optional prompt expansion. Accepts prompt and first frame inputs.
WanV22VideoGenerate.label: Wan v2.2

restrictions.text: Accepts up to 1 image input: first frame.

WanV26VideoGenerate.description: Alibaba's WAN 2.6 generates 5-15 second cinematic clips with multi-shot storytelling support and up to 1080p resolution. Supports both text-to-video and image-to-video modes with prompt expansion.
WanV26VideoGenerate.label: Wan v2.6

restrictions.text: Accepts up to 2 inputs: prompt and first frame (both optional).

WanV30OmniReferenceGenerate.description: Wan 3.0 Omni Reference uses reference images, videos, and audio to carry subjects, motion, and voices into a new 2-30 second scene with synchronized native audio at up to 1080p.
WanV30OmniReferenceGenerate.label: Wan v3.0 Omni Reference

restrictions.text: Requires at least 1 reference input. Accepts up to 10 images, 5 videos, and 5 audio clips (max 20 inputs total). Each reference video must be 1-15 seconds, and reference videos and reference audio are each capped at 15 seconds in total. Frame images cannot be mixed with reference material; use Wan 3.0 for first-frame or first-and-last-frame generation.

WanV30VideoGenerate.description: Wan 3.0 generates 2-30 second video with synchronized native audio at up to 1080p. Generate from text, animate a first frame, or connect first and last frames to fill in the motion between them.
WanV30VideoGenerate.label: Wan v3.0

restrictions.text: Accepts up to 2 image inputs: first frame and end frame. To guide generation with reference images, videos, or audio instead, use Wan 3.0 Omni Reference; frame images and reference material cannot be mixed in one generation.

WavespeedUpscale.description: High-performance AI image upscaler that intelligently increases resolution while preserving details, sharpness, and natural texture. Uses advanced deep learning to restore fine features and eliminate blur or compression artifacts. Supports 2K, 4K, and 8K output resolutions.
WavespeedUpscale.label: Wavespeed Upscale

restrictions.text: Requires exactly 1 image.

WavespeedWatermarkRemover.description: Remove watermarks, logos, captions, lower-thirds, and burned-in subtitles from video using temporal-aware AI inpainting. Automatically detects on-screen overlays and reconstructs the background underneath while keeping motion stable and avoiding flicker. Supports clips up to 10 minutes.
WavespeedWatermarkRemover.label: Watermark & Subtitle Remover

restrictions.text: Requires exactly 1 video input.

ZImageTurboGenerate.description: Lightweight fast text-to-image model with bilingual Chinese/English prompt rendering. Supports flexible resolutions and aspect ratios. Uses text prompts only.
ZImageTurboGenerate.label: Z-Image Turbo
